# Implement block: Aurora Glass Welcome (SwiftUI)

You are adding the "Aurora Glass Welcome" block from Native Cook to the user's iOS app. The block already exists as working SwiftUI code. Your job is to bring it into this project faithfully, not to write a new one that looks similar.

## The block

A welcome screen for an invented aurora-forecast app under a live northern-lights sky. Three curtains of light hang at three depths over a night-blue sky with faint twinkling stars: crisp green-white hems that fold along their length, comb upwards into rays and turn teal, then violet (red-violet on the farthest), above a mountain range standing as a dark silhouette with the light in its wet reflections. A bold "Chase the northern light." climbs out of its lines under a SOLVIND wordmark and a small weather chip. Low on the screen floats a frosted glass forecast card with a hairline edge brightest along the top: tonight's Kp 6.3, the best window, an activity curve that draws itself on with a pulsing marker on the peak, and cloud cover, moonlight and darkness figures; a white Get started pill and a sign-in link sit below. Dragging tilts the card in 3D while a sheen slides across its glass, and the aurora bends towards the finger.

**Motion.** The sky is one runtime shader (Skia in React Native, Metal in SwiftUI, AGSL on Android 13 and later; below Android 13 soft green and violet glows drift over the night instead): three curtains, each a hem wandering with value-noise fbm (4 octaves), a soft-to-crisp edge (0.03, 0.016 and 0.008 of the height for far, middle and near), a body falling off over 0.24, 0.2 and 0.15 of the height plus a bright band near the hem, folds from a sine along the hem, rays from noise stretched 34 to 1.4, and colour from hem to crown over 2.6 times the fall-off; the far and middle curtains are dimmed to 42% and 70% and move 12% and 22% with the finger against 34% for the near one. Colour is tone-mapped with 1 − e^(−1.4c) and dithered by one 8-bit step against banding. The flow moves its noise offsets round circles (0.55 at once and 0.4 at twice the loop), so it returns to the same frame every LOOP of 10 s, and stars twinkle three times a loop. The horizon photo, drawn 1.5 times the screen's width with its top 31% of the height down, is keyed into a silhouette with a colour matrix (alpha 1.6 − 2.5 × luminance), fades in over its top 16% and melts into the night ground over 110 pt. Entrance: the aurora lights up over 1.6 s and the horizon rises 26 pt with it (ease-out 0.23, 1, 0.32, 1); the bar fades in at 0.15 s; the headline lines rise 50 pt out of clipped slots over 0.76 s from 0.26 and 0.36 s; the line of copy at 0.52 s; the card from 0.6 s over 0.85 s, rising 40 pt and growing from 96%; its curve draws on from 0.95 s over 1.15 s (ease-in-out 0.65, 0, 0.35, 1), its area uncovered with it, and the marker springs onto the peak (0.5 s, damping ratio 0.5) and pulses five times a loop; the figures rise 8 pt from 1.15 s, 0.08 s apart; the buttons at 1.0 s; each over 0.6 s unless said. Self-playing, the card yaws 9° × sin(2πt/10) and pitches 4° × sin(4πt/10) under a 900 pt perspective while the aurora's pull point follows at 0.5 + 0.32 × sin of the width. Dragging anywhere tilts the card 0.09° per pt, rubber-banding past 16°, lifts it 1.5% with a soft haptic, and bends the aurora towards the finger (its pull ramps in over 250 ms and out over 1.2 s after release); let go, the card springs flat (700 ms, damping ratio 0.55) carrying the finger's speed. The self-playing tilt hands over at the touch and fades back in over 0.9 s, 3 s after release. A diagonal sheen slides 220 pt against the yaw and 80 pt with the pitch, from 20% opacity flat to full at 16°. The chip's dot pulses five times a loop. The button dips to 0.97 over 110 ms with a selection haptic. Under reduced motion the card does not tilt by itself, the sky flows at half speed and lights up in 0.6 s, nothing rises or draws on (the curve and marker fade in), and a release settles in 300 ms without overshoot.

## Reference source

The block is built and running in the Native Cook source repository. Each link below is a file on GitHub. To read one as plain text, replace `https://github.com/Native-Cook/native-cook/blob/` with `https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Native-Cook/native-cook/` in its address.

### Demo (start here)

- [AuroraGlassWelcomeDemo.swift](https://github.com/Native-Cook/native-cook/blob/main/swift/NativeCook/Blocks/Onboarding/AuroraGlassWelcome/AuroraGlassWelcomeDemo.swift)

### Files of the block

- [AuroraGlassWelcome.metal](https://github.com/Native-Cook/native-cook/blob/main/swift/NativeCook/Blocks/Onboarding/AuroraGlassWelcome/AuroraGlassWelcome.metal)
- [AuroraGlassWelcome.swift](https://github.com/Native-Cook/native-cook/blob/main/swift/NativeCook/Blocks/Onboarding/AuroraGlassWelcome/AuroraGlassWelcome.swift)
- [AuroraGlassWelcomeEngine.swift](https://github.com/Native-Cook/native-cook/blob/main/swift/NativeCook/Blocks/Onboarding/AuroraGlassWelcome/AuroraGlassWelcomeEngine.swift)

### Shared helpers the block uses

- [swift/NativeCook/Shared/ComponentSupport.swift](https://github.com/Native-Cook/native-cook/blob/main/swift/NativeCook/Shared/ComponentSupport.swift)

### Frameworks

It needs no framework beyond SwiftUI.

## Your instructions

_Anything specific to this app goes here: where the block should appear, what to rename, what to change. Left empty, integrate the block as it is._

## How to work

Work like an experienced iOS engineer joining an existing project: learn the app first, read only what you need, decide early how the block fits, then integrate it with as little disruption as possible. Take the steps in order.

**Done means** the block is reachable in the user's app and behaves like the reference in the iOS Simulator or on a device. A SwiftUI preview is useful while you work, but it is not the proof: build and run the app.

**Fidelity.** Bring over the real implementation. Keep its structure, colours, sizes, timings and curves. Change only what this project requires and what "Your instructions" ask for.

If you already learned this project earlier in the conversation, reuse what you know and skip step 2. Learn it again only if the project changed or something you need is missing.

### 1. Check where you are

- You need the project's files and a terminal. If this prompt was pasted into a chat that has neither, stop and say so: it has to be run by a coding agent opened on the project.
- Confirm the project is an iOS app built with Xcode (an `.xcodeproj`, an `.xcworkspace` or a Swift package with an app target). If it is something else, stop, say what you found, and do not create a new app inside it unless the instructions ask for one.

### 2. Learn the host app

- The app target, its deployment target and its Swift version.
- SwiftUI, UIKit or both, and how a screen is shown today: `NavigationStack`, a coordinator, a tab bar, a storyboard.
- How files join the target: a folder the project synchronises, or a file list in the project that you have to extend.
- Conventions: folder layout, naming, where colours, fonts and assets live.
- Type names the app already uses, so the block's types do not collide with them.

### 3. Read the block

- Swift files in a module do not import each other, so the demo alone will not lead you to the rest. The list above names every file of the block: read them all.
- The demo is how the source repository shows the block. Bring over what the demo shows, not the repository's gallery. Anything listed under "Used by the demo only" stays behind.
- Read the block's initialiser and its defaults. The demo may switch on an option that makes the block play by itself for a recording (for example `autoPlay`). Keep the option; leave it off in the user's app unless asked.

### 4. Decide the fit

- The source app targets iOS 17. If the host targets an older system, check each API the block uses and tell the user what would have to change before you lower anything. Do not raise the host's deployment target without asking.
- If a type or function name of the block already exists in the app, rename the block's one, in every file that uses it, and say that you did.
- Shared helpers: copy the ones the block uses next to it, or fold them into the block's files. Do not copy helpers it never calls.
- In a UIKit app, show the block through a `UIHostingController`.

### 5. Bring it in

- Add the block's files to the app target, keeping their names.
- Copy its asset catalogs, loose resources and fonts, and check that the names the code asks for match the names in the bundle: a wrong name compiles and then shows nothing.
- A `.metal` file has to be compiled into the same target as the code that calls its function.
- Keep reduced-motion handling, haptics and accessibility labels as they are in the source.
- Mount the block where the instructions say. With no instructions, add a screen named after the block and make it reachable the way the app's other screens are.

### 6. Run it

- Build the app target for a simulator with `xcodebuild` or the project's own script, and fix every error and new warning the block introduced.
- Run it and use the block: every state, every gesture, light and dark appearance if the block follows them, and once with Reduce Motion on.
- If the build or the simulator fails for a reason outside the block, report the error and ask how to continue.

### 7. Report

- Files added and changed, and anything renamed to avoid a collision.
- How to reach the block in the app.
- Anything that differs from the reference, and why.
